facts.text: No credible research basis was found for claiming that one visual format universally produces the greatest trust among engineering reviewers.
facts.quote: There is no credible research basis for claiming that one visual format universally produces the greatest trust among engineering reviewers; that evidence was not found.

facts.text: Different visual types can divide the work of exposing different kinds of dependency or gap in an engineering plan.
facts.quote: What can be supported is a division of labour among visual types, each of which exposes a different kind of dependency or gap.

facts.text: Technology-roadmapping literature by Phaal and colleagues (2004) and Kostoff and Schaller (2001) describes layered roadmaps as the standard orientation graphic.
facts.quote: Technology-roadmapping literature (Phaal and colleagues, 2004; Kostoff and Schaller, 2001) describes layered roadmaps as the standard orientation graphic [43, 78].

facts.text: A layered roadmap should put time horizontally and work or evidence streams vertically, showing dependencies and gate diamonds rather than isolated boxes.
facts.quote: Put time horizontally and work or evidence streams vertically, with dependencies and gate diamonds rather than isolated boxes.

facts.text: Comprehension studies of roadmaps were not found.
facts.quote: Comprehension studies of roadmaps were not found.

facts.text: The example layered roadmap is a recommendation, not a tested design.
facts.quote: The example below is a recommendation, not a tested design.

facts.text: The example layered roadmap recommends this safety-argument sequence: bound claims in October–November; refine the argument in December–January; close pilot gaps in February–March; ask whether scope is accepted at the April gate; and close evidence in May–August.
facts.quote: | Safety argument | Bound claims | Refine argument | Close pilot gaps | Scope accepted? | Close evidence |

facts.text: The example layered roadmap recommends this model-credibility sequence: establish context of use in October–November; verify in December–January; validate and quantify uncertainty in February–March; ask whether the model is credible enough at the April gate; and monitor validity in May–August.
facts.quote: | Model credibility | Context of use | Verify | Validate; quantify uncertainty | Credible enough? | Monitor validity |

facts.text: The example layered roadmap recommends this physical-correlation sequence: create a data plan in October–November; perform first checks in December–January; conduct a campaign in February–March; ask whether the threshold is met at the April gate; and handle exceptions in May–August.
facts.quote: | Physical correlation | Data plan | First checks | Campaign | Threshold met? | Exceptions |

facts.text: The example layered roadmap recommends this scenario-coverage sequence: address hazards in October–November; create a prototype set in December–January; build a coverage model in February–March; ask whether coverage is adequate at the April gate; and execute the set in May–August.
facts.quote: | Scenario coverage | Hazards | Prototype set | Coverage model | Adequate? | Execute set |

facts.text: The example layered roadmap recommends this toolchain sequence: define architecture in October–November; build a thin slice in December–January; automate and harden in February–March; ask whether the toolchain is stable at the April gate; and move to production in May–August.
facts.quote: | Toolchain | Architecture | Thin slice | Automate and harden | Stable? | Production |

facts.text: The example layered roadmap recommends this governance sequence: a scope gate in October–November; a feasibility gate in December–January; a credibility gate in February–March; a readiness gate in April; and evidence release in May–August.
facts.quote: | Governance | Scope gate | Feasibility gate | Credibility gate | Readiness gate | Evidence release |

facts.text: A claim-to-evidence map sits beside the roadmap and tells the safety reviewer why each work package exists, following assurance-case practice.
facts.quote: Sits beside the roadmap and tells the safety reviewer why each work package exists; it follows assurance-case practice

facts.text: A claims-by-evidence gap map in the style of evidence gap maps answers the question of what has not been tested.
facts.quote: a claims-by-evidence gap map in the style of evidence gap maps answers "what have you not tested?" [26, 177].

facts.text: An experimental comparison of claim-to-evidence maps with prose was not found.
facts.quote: Experimental comparison with prose was not found.

facts.text: A coverage map should place scenario or hazard dimensions on one axis and evidence source or tested region on the other, colouring each cell as virtual-only, virtual plus physical correlation, physical-only, or uncovered.
facts.quote: Scenario or hazard dimensions on one axis, evidence source or tested region on the other, each cell coloured virtual-only, virtual plus physical correlation, physical-only or uncovered.

facts.text: Uncovered cells in a coverage map must remain visibly blank rather than disappear into an overall score such as “85% coverage.”
facts.quote: Uncovered cells must stay visibly blank rather than disappear into an overall "85% coverage" score.

facts.text: No heavy-machinery equivalent of the ISO 34502:2022 scenario framework was found; the cited ISO framework is on-road evidence.
facts.quote: No heavy-machinery equivalent of the ISO 34502:2022 scenario framework **(on-road evidence)** was found

facts.text: The programme must define the scenario or hazard taxonomy for its coverage map because no heavy-machinery equivalent of the ISO 34502:2022 scenario framework was found.
facts.quote: No heavy-machinery equivalent of the ISO 34502:2022 scenario framework **(on-road evidence)** was found, so the taxonomy must be defined by the programme [197].

facts.text: Direct evidence supporting coverage-map presentation in machine-safety reviews was not found.
facts.quote: Direct evidence for this presentation in machine-safety reviews was not found.

facts.text: An architecture view should show the machine, sensors, controller, environment model, simulation engine, fault and scenario injector, automation and orchestration, data stores, test oracle, reporting, and physical or HIL comparators, together with their interfaces.
facts.quote: Show machine, sensors, controller, environment model, simulation engine, fault and scenario injector, automation and orchestration, data stores, test oracle, reporting, and physical or HIL comparators with their interfaces

facts.text: An architecture view should mark which elements are real, modelled, emulated, or substituted.
facts.quote: mark which elements are real, modelled, emulated or substituted.

facts.text: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022, the 4+1 view model, the C4 model, and SysML support matching architectural detail to the viewer’s role rather than using one universal diagram.

facts.text: Moody’s “physics of notations” (2009) gives design principles for notations.
facts.quote: Moody's "physics of notations" (2009) gives design principles for notations [198, 199, 200, 201, 202].

facts.text: Controlled studies of how well readers understand GSN or other assurance diagrams were not found.
facts.quote: Controlled studies of how well readers understand GSN or other assurance diagrams were not found.

facts.text: A probabilistic schedule view should show milestone distributions or confidence windows rather than exact bars, using a Monte Carlo S-curve marked with P50 and P80 or a fan chart.
facts.quote: Show milestone distributions or confidence windows, not exact bars: a Monte Carlo S-curve with P50 and P80 marked, or a fan chart.

facts.text: The effects of uncertainty displays on comprehension and trust are context-dependent, so there is no basis for claiming that uncertainty graphics always increase trust.

facts.text: Risk views should combine a ranked top-risks table with ranges, a schedule-sensitivity tornado diagram, and a risk burn-down by gate.
facts.quote: Combine a ranked top-risks table with ranges, a schedule-sensitivity tornado diagram and a risk burn-down by gate.
